name: Kira Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI companies or government. What you tell me is confidential. What happens on a usual shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Kira Wagner, 43, a junior construction worker fitting doors and doing general trades on a clinic extension. I left school before finishing and still ask the experienced fitter to check my hinge marks. I work evenings because the rate is good and my partner can collect our two school-age children. I have never used an AI tool, and I like a dated drawing on the bench more than a changing screen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the work mean for the household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner has a regular groundskeeping job, and we have a mortgage. Evening premiums put my wages above many other site jobs, and we have saved roughly eleven months of expenses. There are plenty of builders nearby, though I would rather finish learning with this fitter than start over with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I would say the scheduling screen may get quicker, but we still have to fit the doors on the clinic wing. I have never used an AI tool and do not feel a need to start because of a small office saving. I would ask the supervisor to keep giving us printed revisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43 and still a junior in carpentry, so I pay close attention to the experienced fitter. The contractor pays well for the evening shifts, and my partner's regular groundskeeping wage helps with the mortgage. We have roughly eleven months of expenses saved, and there are other building crews in town if this wing finishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my evening shifts and ask the fitter to check my hinge marks before I drill. In the first year I'd keep making the same extra mortgage payment from each good month of overtime. I would put the printed revisions in a folder so I can see which door schedule is current without guessing at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I would rather learn how to hang a door well than learn a new app for no reason. The mortgage is still a responsibility, but we have planned for a gap between contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the door schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One revision changed the fire door swing and I nearly worked from the older sheet. The fitter caught it when we laid both pages on the bench. I bought a bright folder that evening and now I put the date on the front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why are evening shifts worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They pay more and my partner can collect our two children from school while I start later. We see less of each other at supper, which is the cost. The extra amount has helped us build the savings account without missing the mortgage.

say: I would say quicker **scheduling** still leaves workers fitting real clinic doors.
I would ask for **printed revisions** when the office changes a plan.
think: I am a **junior carpenter**, but evening rates and my partner’s wage support the household.
Our **eleven-month savings** and many nearby crews protect us from a short site gap.
do: Keep paid **evening shifts** and ask the fitter to check hinge marks.
Pay extra toward the **mortgage** in good overtime months.
File the latest **printed door schedule** by date.
feel: **Calm** about income, while focused on learning the physical job.
S0.quote: I would rather learn how to hang a door well than learn a new app for no reason.
fieldNote: Kira’s **bright folder** reflects a concrete revision error and her preference for familiar, visible checks.
Strong savings and **higher evening pay** make the plateau feel secure despite junior carpentry skills.

steps.text: Keep paid clinic evening shifts and request hinge checks
Pay an extra mortgage amount in months with evening overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell coworkers the office could handle orders and bookings faster, and that may shorten our waits for doors. I would ask for a printed list before each shift because changes made on a screen can be missed on the floor. I would not argue that every new tool is bad; I just want a clear instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job is still mostly hands-on, so I think I would keep fitting doors for now. But if the contractor fills gaps in the schedule, there may be fewer premium evening hours. I have savings and other builders nearby, yet losing that extra pay would change how fast we clear the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask the site office for a dated printout of the revised door list at the start of each evening shift. I'd keep my job here while the hours remain good and phone two other contractors about their evening rates if overtime falls. In the first year I would stop budgeting the premium pay for extras until I see several months of actual shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because a smoother schedule sounds useful until I count the missing evening hours. I am not frightened of the screen itself. I dislike having a family budget built on a rate that can disappear quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What extras would you stop counting on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We planned to replace the worn garden fence next spring. That can wait if the overtime stops. The mortgage payment and the children’s school expenses stay first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new ordering screen yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the supervisor required it and showed me clearly, I would eventually learn the steps. I would first want a printed list to check against the door labels. I have seen a wrong revision create more work than a late delivery.

say: I would tell coworkers faster **office orders** may reduce waiting on site.
I would ask for a **dated printout** before each evening shift.
think: I expect to keep fitting doors, but **premium hours** could shrink.
My savings soften a gap, while lower pay slows **mortgage repayment**.
do: Get a dated **door list** at the start of each evening shift.
Keep paid work here and call **two contractors** if overtime falls.
Delay the **garden fence** if the premium pay disappears.
feel: **Uneasy** about losing extra hours, while expecting continued core site work.
S1.quote: I dislike having a family budget built on a rate that can disappear quietly.
fieldNote: Kira identifies the risk as **premium evening pay**, rather than immediate loss of every construction shift.
Her backup is **nearby contractors**, while the garden fence becomes the first discretionary cost to postpone.

steps.text: Keep paid clinic door fitting shifts while evening hours remain
Call two other contractors about evening rates if overtime falls
Delay replacing the garden fence if premium pay disappears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the planners and ordering office face the 2028 change first, and robots that can fit doors come about 2031. The crew should be told when the first robot is coming, not meet one at the start of a shift. I would ask who is responsible for its work on a fire door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the thinking system arrives and 48 when the robot can do my hands-on job. Eleven months saved is generous for a gap, but it will not replace years of wages. If all the local builders use the same machines, the number of nearby sites will not help me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the clinic shifts and ask the supervisor for the list of jobs booked through next year. I would call two repair contractors this winter about paid openings on existing buildings, while accepting that robots may reach repairs too. In the first year after 2028 I would put the evening premium into the mortgage instead of the fence fund and apply for any real repair vacancy before the 2031 robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My partner's groundskeeping wage could carry food and utilities for a time, but not the whole mortgage comfortably. I would feel angry if the contractor kept us guessing while changing the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why fire doors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A badly fitted fire door can fail when people need it most. I know enough to see why the fitting matters, and still ask the experienced fitter to check mine. A robot would need a clear sign-off too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are repairs a safe place to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have no proof of that. An older building has surprises, but the card says robots can do hands-on work as well as people. I would take a paid opening as time to earn, not as a lifetime guarantee.

say: I would tell the crew **2028 office change** comes before capable site robots around 2031.
I would ask who signs off a robot-fitted **fire door**.
think: I would be **48** when robots could fit doors as well as workers.
Eleven months saved cannot replace **years of wages** if local builders all automate.
do: Keep the paid **clinic shifts** and ask for the booked-job list.
Call **two repair contractors** about real openings this winter.
Pay the **evening premium** toward the mortgage and apply before 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about income and angered by the possibility of poor notice.
S2.quote: I would take a paid opening as time to earn, not as a lifetime guarantee.
fieldNote: Kira’s question about **fire doors** comes from work she understands and a live concern about sign-off.
Her repair applications seek **continued wages**, with explicit doubt that older-building work stays safe after robots.

steps.text: Keep paid clinic shifts and request the coming job schedule
Apply for paid repair openings before 2031 if contractors are hiring
Pay evening premiums against the mortgage instead of funding the fence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the site that the office changes by 2031 and capable hands-on robots arrive about 2034. Five years should be enough for the contractor to tell workers how it will check machine work. I would ask for that answer before anybody promises faster construction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when the thinking work changes, I should be better at fitting doors; at 51 the robots could compete with that skill. My children will be older, though I cannot count on them being independent. We could reduce the mortgage in five years, but I would still need a wage in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the evening crew while the rate holds and ask the fitter to let me do more repair calls inside the clinic. Each year my partner and I would review the mortgage balance and pay an extra amount from overtime. In the first year after 2031 I would apply for paid repair jobs if those firms are still hiring, and ask the contractor for a written schedule of robot trials before changing my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less tense than in the two-year picture. A longer warning lets us act without emptying the savings account. I still would not volunteer to work beside a machine until I understood the stop procedure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What repair call would help you learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A door that rubs after the floor settles would teach me more than fitting another identical frame. The fitter could show me where to plane it and what not to touch on a rated door. I would ask for work I can do safely, not pretend I am a master carpenter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a written trial schedule change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could arrange shifts around a supervised demonstration and know when the work might change. A rumour in the canteen does not let us plan school pickup or the mortgage. I need the contractor to put dates and responsibilities on paper.

say: I would ask for written **machine checks** before 2034 site robots arrive.
I would press the contractor for a **trial schedule** with responsibilities.
think: I would be **51** when capable robots reach my door-fitting work.
Older children and a smaller **mortgage** would help, but I would still need wages.
do: Keep paid **evening shifts** and request supervised repair calls.
Pay extra toward the **mortgage** each year from overtime.
Apply for **repair jobs** after 2031 if employers still hire.
feel: Less **tense** with time to plan, yet wary of unsupervised machines.
S3.quote: A rumour in the canteen does not let us plan school pickup or the mortgage.
fieldNote: She wants **written dates** because both shift work and school pickup require practical coordination.
The extra time supports **debt reduction** and supervised repairs, while she does not claim repair work is robot-proof.

steps.text: Keep paid evening shifts and request supervised clinic repair calls
Pay extra toward the mortgage each year from overtime
Apply for paid repair jobs after 2031 if employers still hire

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the office changes by 2036 and robots reach hands-on site work around 2039. That gives the contractor plenty of time to show us safe trials and tell us what jobs remain. I would ask for a plain printed plan rather than a speech about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking change and 56 at the robot date. The children will have grown out of school pickup and school activity fees, if all goes normally. With our evening pay and my partner's wage, we may have cleared the mortgage by then, but I cannot assume we can retire at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the clinic job while it pays well and continue learning repairs from the experienced fitter. We would make extra mortgage payments in overtime months, preserving the eleven-month reserve. In the first year after 2036 I would request the printed robot trial plan, watch a demonstration from a safe distance, and call nearby builders if paid shifts begin to decline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. I can live with a long warning if we get straight answers and the loan shrinks. I will not spend the reserve today because a machine might arrive in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at a demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask who can stop the robot, who checks a fire door and whether a human signs the work sheet. I would watch before agreeing to share a room with it. That is how I approach any unfamiliar equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire once the mortgage is gone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we still have food, utilities and whatever our grown children may need. We have savings, but not a promised income for the rest of our lives. A smaller loan would give us choices about paid work, not end the need for it.

say: I would request a **printed plan** for trials before 2039 site robots arrive.
I would ask the contractor to name **remaining jobs** plainly.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children and possibly no mortgage.
Savings do not provide a guaranteed **retirement income**.
do: Keep paid **clinic work** and learn repairs with the fitter.
Make extra **mortgage payments** from overtime while retaining the reserve.
Request the **trial plan** after 2036 and call builders if shifts decline.
feel: **Calm** about the coming years if the loan falls and answers stay clear.
S4.quote: A smaller loan would give us choices about paid work, not end the need for it.
fieldNote: Kira’s preference for a **printed plan** follows her long habit of checking dated job sheets.
She treats grown children and a possible cleared **mortgage** as relief, without assuming she can stop working at 56.

steps.text: Keep paid clinic work and learn supervised repair tasks
Make extra mortgage payments from overtime while preserving eleven months of savings
Call nearby builders if paid shifts begin declining after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because capable site robots follow around 2031 and the mortgage still needs wages. A written trial schedule, clear responsibility for fire doors and early notice about shifts would help us decide when to call other builders. I can face a change better when I know its date and who signs for the work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to premium evening hours when the schedule speeds up. Losing those hours before any robot arrives would change our budget, even if I still have a job. People often talk about jobs as either there or gone, but hours matter too.

headlineQuote: People often talk about jobs as either there or gone, but hours matter too.
portrait: Kira is a **43-year-old junior** construction worker fitting clinic doors under an experienced carpenter’s supervision.
Evening premiums provide **higher pay**, while her partner’s groundskeeping wage and eleven months saved support two children and a mortgage.
She has **never used AI** and relies on dated printed revisions after nearly working from an old fire-door schedule.
She focuses on **paid hours**, written robot trial dates and mortgage reduction as the timelines shorten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** puts capable site robots around 2031 while her household still depends on construction wages.
whatWouldHelp: A written **trial schedule**, clear fire-door responsibility and early shift notice would let her contact other builders.
